voyage.name: Seattle CityPASS
voyage.price: $127 for adult, $97 for children (ages 5-12), plus tax and a $2 processing fee per ticket
voyage.content: A discount pass that includes admission to five attractions for half the normal fee combined. You are entitled to up to two visits (within 24 hours) to the Space Needle and a visit to the Seattle Aquarium. You also get three choices of an Argosy Cruises Harbor Tour, admission to the Museum of Pop Culture, the Woodland Park Zoo, the Pacific Science Center the Museum of Flight, or Chihuly Garden & Glass. A CityPASS is

voyage.name: Kenmore Air
voyage.content: 20 minute plane tours over Seattle that are narrated by the pilot, with spectacular views of the city. Tours begin and end at the west side of Lake Union. Reservations required.

voyage.name: Argosy Cruises
voyage.price: Harbor cruise $30.50. Locks cruise $42.50, bus connection $5 additional. Discounts for kids 4-12 and seniors
voyage.hours: Cruise schedule varies by season. Ticket booth: Daily 10AM-4:05PM
voyage.content: Boat tour company with special dinner and sightseeing cruises. The most common tour is the hour-long Harbor Cruise on Elliott Bay, which offers excellent views of the Space Needle, Downtown skyline, freight harbor, and usually some sea lions, with a barrage of informative commentary about local history or interesting ships or cargo passing through that day. The Locks Cruise is a 2-hour one-way trip (in alternating di

voyage.name: Waterways Cruises
voyage.hours: Cruises on Sat-Sun and sometimes Fri; see schedule online. Office: Mon-Fri 9AM-5PM
voyage.content: Luxury dining cruises touring Lake Union and Lake Washington. Regular cruises include 2-hour weekend brunch and Sunday supper buffets, and a 2½-hour four-course dinner (business casual attire).

voyage.name: Chinese Lunar New Year
voyage.content: Numerous stalls and performances, and don't forget to partake in all the cheap food!

voyage.name: Seattle International Film Festival
voyage.content: One of the largest film festivals in North America, showing international cinema. Watch indie films at Seattle area screens and vote for your favorite; each category winner receives a Golden Space Needle trophy. SIFF also screens films year-round at its venues.

voyage.name: Northwest Folklife Festival
voyage.price: Free ($10 donation per person per day encouraged)
voyage.content: A more low-key and local version of Bumbershoot, mainly family-friendly.

voyage.name: Fremont Fair
voyage.hours: a weekend in mid or late June
voyage.content: Home of the Solstice Parade (including the nude bike ride), and a really fun drunken time all over Fremont. Vendors, bad live music and eclectic crowds at the bars make for an interesting time. Friends who live in Fremont become especially valuable for a place to crash during the fair.

voyage.name: Seattle PrideFest
voyage.hours: A weekend in June or July
voyage.content: One of the biggest gay pride festivals in the country. Food carts, beer gardens, adult theme performances, and the eagerly anticipated Pride Parade.

voyage.name: Bite of Seattle
voyage.content: Part of Seafair festivities. Enjoy some of the best delicacies of Seattle.

voyage.name: Capitol Hill Block Party
voyage.content: Yearly live music event held on Capitol Hill over a weekend in mid-summer (usually the end of July). Consists primarily of local independent bands of various styles, coupled with some bigger name independent label acts.

voyage.name: Seafair
voyage.content: Seattle's biggest festival, signifying the arrival of summer. Neighborhood events such as parades and street fairs run throughout the festival, with the downtown Torchlight Parade in late July. Seafair culminates in early August when hydroplane races and the Blue Angels bring loud, fast boats and planes to Lake Washington.

voyage.name: Bumbershoot
voyage.content: Seattle's largest music and arts festival, featuring dozens of local and world-class musical acts.

voyage.name: Night Market & Autumn Moon Festival
voyage.content: Chinese festival of food and outdoor market.

voyage.name: Luminata
voyage.content: A festival of lights at Green Lake, including a procession from the old Aqua Theatre to a clearing about 3/4 mile north.

voyage.name: Festál Cultural Center
voyage.content: Celebrate the world with festivals from about 25 countries represented, one country nearly every 2 weeks.

voyage.name: Olympic Sculpture Park
voyage.hours: Opens 30 minutes before sunrise, closes 30 minutes after sunset
voyage.content: of green space on Seattle’s waterfront with a collection of monumental sculptures.

voyage.name: Seattle Art Museum
voyage.price: Suggested admission: $19.50 adult, $17.50 senior/military, $2.50 students/youth, children 12 and under free. Admission is free on first Thursday of the month
voyage.hours: Tue Wed Fri-Sun 10AM-5PM, Thu 10AM-9PM, closed Mon
voyage.content: The museum displays a good assortment of art from the Pacific Northwest and around the world. Though the permanent exhibitions only occasionally delve deeply into a specific subject (such as the enormous variety of pieces in the porcelain room), extensive special exhibitions fill the gap. Tours available.

voyage.name: Seattle Public Library-Central Library
voyage.content: A dramatic glass and steel structure in the heart of Downtown, designed by Rem Koolhaas. This is not an average public library and has become a tourist destination in its own right. A popular way to experience the unique architecture of the building is to take an elevator to the 10th floor, the highest observation deck in the building. From here you can walk down to the main floor through the Book Spiral; the core of

voyage.name: Sky View Observatory
voyage.price: $22 adults, $19 seniors and military with ID, $16.for kids 5 to 13
voyage.hours: Daily 10AM-8PM (check website for extended summer hours and special hours for holidays)
voyage.content: This observatory sits on the 73rd floor of the Columbia Center, one of the tallest buildings on the West Coast and the tallest public observation deck in the Pacific Northwest, sitting 932 feet (284.2 meters) above the ground and more than 330 feet taller than the Space Needle. Great views are offered from the top and some people claim the view is better from here than from the Space Needle. Another advantage over th

voyage.name: Tilikum Place
voyage.content: Etymologically meaning "welcome" in the native Chinook language, Tilikum is home to a statue of Chief Seattle, the chief of the Duwamish tribe that gives this city its name. Sit in the park or in the Tilikum Place Cafe's outdoor seating and enjoy views of the Space Needle while sipping a coffee or enjoying a lunch, and watch the monorail go by.

voyage.name: Miner's Landing at Pier 57
voyage.content: Named for once being the main departure point during the Seattle gold rush, Miner's Landing now hosts a food court and a variety of gourmet restaurants, a sports merchandise store, a carousel for kids and the Seattle Great Wheel.

voyage.name: Seattle Great Wheel
voyage.hours: Hours vary by season; closes Fri Sat at midnight, 11PM (July–September) or 10PM (other months) all other days
voyage.content: Rising 175 feet in the air, this Ferris wheel offers a 15-minute ride in one of the wheel's 42 gondolas, each of which can hold up to 8 people. You'll get a wonderful view of the Seattle waterfront, the Downtown skyline, as well as the Puget Sound, the snow-covered Olympics, and the green city hills.

voyage.name: Seattle Aquarium
voyage.price: $21.95 adults, $14.95 children (4-12), children 3 and under free
voyage.address: 1483 Alaskan Way (on Pier 59 on the waterfront)
voyage.content: Showcases native fish and mammals of the Pacific Northwest. Among the highlights are the Windows on Washington (WOW) exhibit, two touch tanks featuring animals of the inland sea and outer coast, and a display that holds two giant pacific octopuses, gill sharks and Pacific coral reefs. The outdoor exhibit upstairs features a collection of birds, harbor and Northern fur seals, as well as river and sea otters. At a sepa

voyage.name: Argosy Cruises
voyage.price: Prices vary according to your itinerary; $23.75 for harbor cruise
voyage.content: Offers special dinner and sightseeing cruises. The most common tour visitors take is the hour-long journey on Elliott Bay, which gives you an excellent view not just of the Space Needle and the Downtown skyline, but the freight harbor to the south as well.

voyage.name: Seattle Convention Center
voyage.alt: formerly the Washington State Convention Center
voyage.content: The largest events space in the state, and the host of PAX West, Emerald City Comic Con, Sakura-Con, the Northwest Flower and Garden Show, and many others. The Arch building spans across Pike Street, 8th Avenue, and I-5. The Summit building, opened in 2023, is a block north.

voyage.name: Benaroya Hall
voyage.hours: Free tours offered Tue and Fri at noon and 1PM
voyage.content: An aesthetically and acoustically beautiful new concert hall. The official home of the Seattle Symphony Orchestra, it also houses other classical and performing arts roadshows.

voyage.name: 5th Avenue Theatre
voyage.content: The main Seattle venue for touring Broadway musical shows; also hosts a number of original musicals that later head to Broadway.

voyage.name: Unexpected Productions
voyage.content: Seattle's longest running improv theater.

voyage.name: Seattle International Film Festival (SIFF)
voyage.content: One of the largest film festivals in North America. Screenings are at the SIFF Cinema Uptown (3 screens), the SIFF Cinema Downtown, and two venues at Seattle Center, the SIFF Film Center and the PACCAR IMAX Theater.

voyage.name: SIFF Cinema Downtown
voyage.content: One of just three Cinerama theaters in the world, this cinema shows art, indie, and foreign films and documentaries.

voyage.name: Pike Place Market
voyage.hours: Building open 9AM-7PM daily. Produce stands and fish markets from 7AM-4PM, Crafts market from 11AM-4PM. Restaurants and other merchants vary

voyage.name: DeLaurenti Food & Wine
voyage.content: Established in 1946 as an importer of specialty Italian and Mediterranean foods, with an extensive collection of pastas, cheeses, jarred vegetables and high-end wines.

voyage.name: Made in Washington
voyage.content: Sells all kinds of souvenirs exclusive to Washington state. Along with the usual coffee mugs and fridge magnets, they also sell glass sculptures you can find at the Chihuly Arts and Glass, baked salmon, artisan chocolates and the rain-globe, an equivalent to a snow globe but adapted to suit the stereotypical Seattle drizzle. They also have another shop in Westlake Center.

voyage.name: Metsker Maps
voyage.content: One of the last remaining map stores in the U.S., with a presence in Seattle since the 1930s. The store is covered wall-to-wall with all kinds of maps local and worldwide, the shelves are crammed with globes and atlases and travel books, and cabinets of posters and prints are rewarding to sift through.

voyage.name: Pike Place Fish Market
voyage.content: Founded in 1930, known for its fishmongers that throw orders across the shop before wrapping for customers. The repeated shouting of fish orders started as a prank, but became an entertaining tradition.

voyage.name: Gum Wall
voyage.content: In 1991, patrons of a neighboring theater started sticking used chewing gum to this wall. The gum persisted despite repeated cleanings, so the market gave up and embraced it as an icky tourist attraction. It is still subject to sporadic deep cleans, to keep the inches-thick crust of fermenting sugar and saliva from digesting the bricks.

voyage.name: Pacific Place Mall
voyage.content: This 5-floor shopping mall is anchored by a large AMC movie theater and Din Tai Fung restaurant on the top floors. While the mall once featured upscale brands, it is now a little sparse, with mostly galleries and independent businesses.

voyage.name: Westlake Center
voyage.content: A small 4-floor shopping mall at the southern terminus of the Seattle Center Monorail (third floor) and connected to Westlake Station (in the basement), with a food court and a handful of retailers.

voyage.name: H Mart
voyage.content: This upscale Korean chain operates the only supermarket in the district.

voyage.name: Target
voyage.content: A small, urban-footprint outpost of the major home goods chain.

voyage.name: The 5 Point Cafe
voyage.content: Seattle's oldest restaurant, serving huge portions of American comfort food since 1929. The full menu is served 24 hours every day. Full bar with stiff drinks, over 25 local beers and liquors. Great jukebox and an eclectic mix of regulars and locals, tourists, politicians, young hipsters, freaks and grouchy old men. Free wifi. Outdoor seating. This is a true piece of Seattle history not to be missed.

voyage.name: Biscuit Bitch
voyage.content: The b-word is in every single item on the menu, and this excellent breakfast place is a siren call to those seeking hangover relief, providing burgers (replace the bun with a biscuit) sandwiches (replace the bread with a biscuit), and typical Southern style food.

voyage.name: Ivar's Acres Of Clams
voyage.content: Smoked salmon plate-lunch and fish-n-chips served outdoors at a scenic waterfront location. Ordering at the walk-up counter outside is inexpensive. Please do not feed ducks and seagulls as human food is harmful for birds! Good food, but pretty touristy.

voyage.name: Beecher's Handmade Cheese
voyage.price: Prices per cheese vary, but a piece weighing 0.5 lb generally costs $10
voyage.content: A library of artisan cheese from Pacific Northwest farms, as well as some handmade cheese in the factory next door, worth bringing home as a Seattle souvenir. Try some free samples and be sure to get some of their mac and cheese.

voyage.name: The Crumpet Shop
voyage.content: Get a crumpet, a griddle cake originated from England, made with organic ingredients, sweet or savory with a number of toppings.

voyage.name: Ellenos Greek Yogurt
voyage.content: A bit expensive compared to its supermarket counterparts, but richer in flavor and milk, making this a local favorite. Often has long lines, but they move quickly and the owner is generous with free samples.

voyage.name: Jack's Fish Spot
voyage.content: A good place to get seafood, especially dungeness crabs. Market-like atmosphere, seating in stools, and they can cook what you buy.

voyage.name: Pike Place Chowder
voyage.content: One of the most famous restaurants at Pike Place Market. Selections of exceptional chowder, as well as sandwiches and seafood cocktails.

voyage.name: Pike Place Chowder
voyage.content: Usually has long lines (up to 30 minutes) due to the fact this location is more well-known. Has more choices of chowder. Seats quickly fill up!

voyage.name: Piroshky Piroshky
voyage.content: A very popular eatery, specializing in their namesake Russian pastries. They have many varieties from which to choose. The smoked salmon, the cheese, onion and garlic roll, and the apple cinnamon roll are all excellent. Be prepared for long lines and out of stock items if you come in late!

voyage.name: Cafe Campagne
voyage.content: Country French cuisine.

voyage.name: Matt's in the Market
voyage.hours: Mon-Sat lunch 11:30AM-2:30PM, dinner 5:30PM-10PM; happy hour Saturdays 5PM-7PM
voyage.content: Charming market ambiance and tasty seafood selections make for a fine low-key dining experience at this small spot.

voyage.name: Palace Kitchen
voyage.content: Tom Douglas' upscale saloon is a hit any time of day.

voyage.name: Serious Pie
voyage.content: Regular and specialty Neapolitan style pizza in one of the best pizza restaurants in Seattle. This small space gets overwhelmed with customers around mealtimes.

voyage.name: Le Pichet
voyage.content: An excellent French bistro. Try the roast chicken.

voyage.name: Ruth's Chris Steakhouse
voyage.content: Side dishes served on a per-table basis, so make sure you can agree with your companions! Skip the happy hour.

voyage.name: The Metropolitan Grill
voyage.content: Caters to those with fat wallets, with massive portions, classic steakhouse ambiance, and top-grade beef.

voyage.name: Purple Cafe & Wine Bar
voyage.hours: Mon-Thu 11AM-11PM, Fri 11AM-midnight, Sat noon-midnight, Sun noon-11PM
voyage.content: Has an extensive wine list and some of Seattle's best food. Don't forget to try the salted caramels for dessert.

voyage.name: Elliott's Oyster House
voyage.hours: Sun-Thu 11AM-10PM, Fri Sat 11AM-11PM, happy hour Mon-Fri 3-6PM
voyage.content: Seafood restaurant that's most famous for fresh oysters. In addition, the menu has various seafood to choose from, such as king salmon, sockeye, dungeness crab, king crab, yellowfin ahi tuna, you name it. Happy hour is affordable, with chef's choice of fresh oysters and other deals. The restaurant is right by the dock and the view is fantastic during the summer when you can sit outside.

voyage.name: Cyclops
voyage.content: Good, hip (but not ultra-hip) bar, and not a bad restaurant either. Interesting neo-retro decor. The Ace Hotel is upstairs. Excellent breakfast.

voyage.name: Owl N' Thistle
voyage.content: A great Irish bar. A house band, nice regulars, and halibut burger to die for. Happy hour is M-F 3-7PM.

voyage.name: The Pink Door
voyage.content: Reasonably good Italian restaurant, but it's a better bar, with a rather romantic European market ambiance and a trellis-covered outdoor deck. Occasional cabaret-style live entertainment, no cover.

voyage.name: Shorty's
voyage.content: Classic pinball games and Coney Island hot dogs, decorated with creepy clowns. Be sure to check out the Trophy Lounge hidden in the back.

voyage.name: Diller's Room
voyage.content: Classic cocktail bar with a historic vibe and extensive drink selection. Happy hour is from 4PM to 6PM with $1 off drinks and $12 pizza.

voyage.name: Original Starbucks
voyage.content: Who would have thought, when this unassuming place opened in 1971, that it would give rise to a global empire? Now flocks of tourists crowd the oldest existing Starbucks. (The true first location was one block north; it moved here when that building was torn down in 1977.) The long line gets you exactly the same drinks you can get at every other location. If you're not a true fan, check out the bare-chested mermaid w

voyage.name: Ace Hotel
voyage.price: Shared bath rooms from $120, deluxe from $200
voyage.content: Budget hotel in the Belltown area. Rooms have an option of shared bath. Minimum furniture and quaint.

voyage.name: City Hostel Seattle
voyage.content: Warm friendly accommodation. Private room available. Free breakfast and Wi-fi. All rooms have murals painted by local artists. $25 dorms.

voyage.name: Green Tortoise Hostel
voyage.content: Has a view of the Puget Sound and the Market, 30 bunk rooms in the elegantly restored Elliot Hotel Building. Free Internet stations and Wi-Fi, free dinner 3 nights a week, and free breakfast every morning. The Green Tortoise is a Seattle backpacker institution that also runs festive low-budget bus tours to Mexico and Central America.

voyage.name: Hotel Five Seattle
voyage.content: Its namesake comes from the site of the hotel at Fifth Avenue, below the monorail tracks. Urban-designed rooms. Complimentary shuttle and bike to roam the city.

voyage.name: La Quinta Inn & Suites Seattle Downtown
voyage.content: Very close to Seattle Center and the downtown shopping core. High-speed internet in rooms and free breakfast included.

voyage.name: Belltown Inn
voyage.content: This little establishment at the heart of Belltown offers kitchenette on every room. Rooms only have fans for summer.

voyage.name: Executive Hotel Pacific
voyage.content: A small hotel in the Belltown area. Standard rooms have small bathrooms, deluxe are slightly larger, suites' bedrooms are perfect for a family and features free Internet and newspaper.

voyage.name: Hotel Max
voyage.content: In the heart of downtown, offers an artistic setting for both business and leisure travelers.

voyage.name: Mayflower Park Hotel
voyage.content: Built in 1927, the centrally-located hotel retains its classical colors on most of its interior, with modern amenities in the rooms such as flat-screen TV and coffee machine. Wi-Fi is complimentary.

voyage.name: Palladian Hotel
voyage.content: A boutique hotel, developed by Kimpton, adopts a European flair. Every room is equipped with a yoga mat and a daily social (wine) hour is available at the hotel's classic bar.

voyage.name: Renaissance Seattle Hotel
voyage.content: A full service hotel in the heart of downtown.

voyage.name: The Roosevelt Hotel
voyage.content: Another boutique and historic option at Belltown.

voyage.name: Warwick Seattle
voyage.content: One of the few budget options in the middle of downtown. Rooms have a view of either the skyline or the Space Needle, added with a Juliet balcony.

voyage.name: The Alexis Royal Sonesta Hotel Seattle
voyage.content: This art-themed hotel has original works throughout the lobby and in the rooms. Furthermore, it sports a big old Dale Chihuly glass piece in the lobby.

voyage.name: The Edgewater
voyage.content: Near the Pike Place Market, right on the water, and famous for three things: you could at one time literally fish right out of your window, it was the site of a notorious Led Zeppelin incident, and the Beatles stayed here during their 1964 tour. Rooms either face the city with no great view other than the Space Needle, or face the water. These latter rooms enjoy the non-stop action of the ferries and cruise liners in

voyage.name: The Fairmont Olympic
voyage.content: The only hotel in the Northwest to win a five-diamond award. Pulls off grand and luxurious perfectly, is in the middle of downtown.

voyage.name: Hilton Motif Seattle
voyage.content: Distinctive downtown hotel featuring modern lifestyle amenities, concierge, restaurants and lounges, meeting venues, business & fitness centers, and Seattle's largest rooftop dining patio - a unique Seattle Lodging experience.

voyage.name: Hotel 1000
voyage.content: New high-tech, boutique style hotel in downtown.

voyage.name: Hotel Andra
voyage.content: A hotel of a local brand with a luxury and modern touch. Rooms have private bars and ironing boards, with plush Turkish towels and Swedish bath amenities. The in-house Mediterranean restaurant is managed by the locally-renowned restaurateur Tom Douglas.

voyage.name: Hotel Monaco Seattle
voyage.content: Centrally located in the historic Pike Place Market downtown, facing the waterfront and Elliott Bay. Short walk to Seattle Art Museum, Benaroya Hall, Pioneer Square, Westlake Center, and lots of dining and shopping.

voyage.name: Pan Pacific Hotel Seattle
voyage.content: This pet-friendly property offers an array of luxury fully furnished rooms and suites equipped with all modern amenities. Facilities include a business center and a fitness center.

voyage.name: Sheraton Grand Seattle
voyage.content: Immediately adjacent to the convention center.

voyage.name: W Seattle
voyage.content: For the terminally hip traveler. Decorated in a stunning palette of black, black, silver, cream, and black.

voyage.name: The Westin Seattle
voyage.content: Perhaps the hotel that has the most rooms in the city. Standard luxurious Westin-style hospitality. It is linked by a skybridge that connects with Westlake Center.

voyage.name: Grand Opera House
voyage.content: Formerly the city's leading theater. Only its exterior survives as the shell of a parking garage.

voyage.name: Klondike Gold Rush National Historic Park - Seattle Unit
voyage.hours: Daily 9AM-5PM except Thanksgiving, Christmas, and New Year's Day
voyage.content: A key attraction in the Pioneer Square area, this is the Seattle branch of the Klondike Gold Rush National Historical Park, the remainder of which is in Alaska. The site highlights the city's key role as the "Gateway to the Gold Fields" for most of the Klondike stampeders of 1897-1898. National Park Service Rangers and volunteers staff the museum and can provide information and perspective not only on the gold rush b

voyage.name: Nihonmachi Alley
voyage.content: Japantown (Nihonmachi) once stretched 20 blocks, but the residents were forced into internment camps during World War II, and Nihonmachi never fully recovered. This alley features murals and exhibits of four landmark businesses that persisted after incarceration.

voyage.name: Seattle Buddhist Church
voyage.content: In the summer the community hosts a Japanese bon odori festival on the street out front.

voyage.name: Smith Tower
voyage.price: Self tour and observatory: adults $27, seniors/military $24, students/children 5-13 $21, under 5 Free, locals with Washington state ID $18. Guided 45 minute tour is additional
voyage.hours: Mon-Wed Noon-7PM, Thu and Sun Noon-8PM, Fri and Sat Noon-9PM
voyage.content: Built in 1914, the Smith Tower was Seattle's first skyscraper, and the tallest building on the West Coast for nearly half a century before being overtaken by the Space Needle. Uniformed attendants operate the old copper and brass elevators from which you can peer into the different floors and offices as you ascend, an experience most people today have probably only witnessed in old movies. The outdoor Observatory on

voyage.name: Wing Luke Museum of the Asian Pacific American Experience
voyage.content: The first Smithsonian affiliate in the Pacific Northwest, this museum features exhibits and programs related to pan-Asian American art, history, and culture. Admission includes a first-come-first-served guided tour of the preserved rooms in its historic 1910 building: an import grocery store, rooms of a hotel and a Chinese family association (allow 45-60 minutes). Neighborhood walking tours are also offered on weeken

voyage.name: Hing Hay Park
voyage.content: A small park in the center of Chinatown. Though you're not too likely to see old folks doing tai chi or playing checkers, it still has character.

voyage.name: Occidental Park
voyage.address: Occidental Ave between Main St and Washington St
voyage.content: This urban park is best known for its four totem poles carved by local artist Duane Pasco. It also has bocce courts, ping pong and foosball tables.

voyage.name: Pioneer Square
voyage.content: Pioneer Square proper is just a small corner park that's often occupied by homeless folks, but generally safe during the day.

voyage.name: Waterfall Garden
voyage.content: This small, tranquil park features a 22-foot high waterfall cascading over granite boulders. The park occupies the site where two 19-year olds, James Casey and Claude Ryan, began a messenger service in 1907 in the basement of a tavern, which eventually grew up to become United Parcel Service (UPS). The Annie E. Casey Foundation, started by James Casey and his siblings in honor of their mother, created the park and ma

voyage.name: Art Walk
voyage.content: The Art Walk is almost synonymous with Pioneer Square and takes place on the first Thursday of every month. Galleries are open until 9PM. Show up early for the free wine and hors d'oeuvres.

voyage.name: Seattle Pinball Museum
voyage.content: A pinball machine museum where all the machines are on free play once you pay admission. There is soda and beer available.

voyage.name: Theatre Off Jackson
voyage.content: A venue for cutting-edge theatrical productions.

voyage.name: Bill Speidel's Underground Tour
voyage.hours: Apr-Sep: daily 9AM-7PM, Oct-Mar: daily 10AM-6PM. Tours on the hour; Jun-Aug: also on the half-hour daily 9:30AM-4:30AM
voyage.content: The original Underground tour. Tours last 75 minutes, including a 15 minute introduction.

voyage.name: Beneath the Streets
voyage.content: Groups are limited to 25 people for a more personal experience. Tours last 60 minutes. Spanish language tours available by appointment.

voyage.name: Beneath the Streets' Red Light District Tour
voyage.content: An adults-only tour with a focus on the "underside" of underground history: prostitution, gambling, drinking and vice. 18 and older. Tours last 90 minutes.

voyage.name: Chinese Lunar New Year
voyage.content: Numerous stalls and performances, and don't forget to partake in all the cheap food!

voyage.name: Night Market & Autumn Moon Festival
voyage.content: Chinese festival of food and outdoor market.

voyage.name: Uwajimaya Village
voyage.content: The commercial, if not cultural, hub of the International District is Uwajimaya Village, a huge Japanese supermarket with many smaller eateries and a branch of the Kinokuniya bookstore. If you need anything at all from Japan while in Seattle, this is the place to find it.

voyage.name: Kinokuniya
voyage.content: A branch of the international Japanese bookstore, crammed full of books from and about Japan as well as other merchandise. Stationery, plushies, K-pop CDs, and calligraphy supplies are just a few of the things you can find in the jam-packed aisles here.

voyage.name: Uwajimaya
voyage.content: An enormous and well-known Japanese supermarket, in business since 1928. The grocery store offers specialty items for almost all forms of Asian cooking. They have great produce, though not always the best prices. But most importantly, they have obscure items like kaffir lime leaves or entire lotus roots, labeled in English. An area on the side has Asian kitchen appliances like rice cookers, kitchenwares including a l

voyage.name: E-Jae Pak Mor
voyage.content: Specializes in pak mor, steamed rice flour dumplings or wraps served as street food in Thailand. You can have them served up in a range of soups and noodle dishes from a menu that's quite unlike other Thai food available in the states.

voyage.name: Fort St. George
voyage.content: A restaurant/bar that serves homey Japanese food and pseudo-Western Japanese dishes like spaghetti with cod roe and curry rice. Popular with exchange students and occasional Seattle Mariners.

voyage.name: Pho Bac
voyage.content: An odd, red boat-shaped shack serving Vietnamese noodle soup. Don't ask for a menu; the only choices are regular or large, and what kind of beef you want.

voyage.name: Rojo’s Mexican Food
voyage.content: Flavorful tacos and burritos made entirely from plant-based ingredients.

voyage.name: Tat's Deli
voyage.hours: Mon-Fri 8AM-3PM, Sat 11AM-5:30PM, Sun open 3 hours before any Seahawks, Sounders, or Mariners matches
voyage.content: East Coast style deli specializing in hoagies, including the delightful pastrami (dubbed Tastrami) and Philly cheesesteak with more varieties of cheese and wit's.

voyage.name: Uwajimaya Village Food Hall
voyage.hours: Hours vary by restaurant, generally daily 10AM-8PM; food court and grocery store Mon-Sat 8AM-10PM, Sun 9AM-9PM
voyage.content: The food court of the Uwajimaya grocery store features 12 stands serving Asian cuisine, from Hawaiian BBQ to Hong Kong style baked goods and everything in-between, though the Thai offerings are not so good. The Chinese steam tables offer reliable, Western-style treats in large quantities for cheap. There aren't any real Japanese offerings, but just inside the grocery store, the deli to the right has plenty of sushi a

voyage.name: World Pizza
voyage.content: Very good vegetarian pizza place (a tasty vegan pizza is also available; call ahead to request it). The place also serves espresso, wine and Manny's Pale Ale on tap. World Pizza's signature pizza features roasted potatoes, garlic, rosemary and Gorgonzola.

voyage.name: Jade Garden
voyage.content: Local favorite for dim sum. While very popular, don't let the seemingly long wait for a table sway you -- the line usually takes less than 30 minutes.

voyage.name: Boiling Point
voyage.content: Hotpot style dining with your very own seemingly large pot and soup, with as much add-ons as you want. They also offer macaron ice cream.

voyage.name: Canton Wonton House
voyage.content: Hong Kong-style noodle soup and congee (jook); great with a side order of Chinese donuts (you tiau). Very inexpensive.

voyage.name: Ping's Dumpling and Tea House
voyage.content: Northern Chinese dumplings are perfect for sharing with a group. The different types of dumplings come with a multitude of fillings and prepared in various ways. While there are several other chains for dumplings (including the international Din Tai Fung and local Dough Zone), Ping's is an independent shop that's more homey and a bit cheaper.

voyage.name: Purple Dot Cafe
voyage.content: This is not a fusion restaurant, but rather a Macau style restaurant. Which explains why you can order your Hong Kong style dishes with spaghetti and cream sauce. Purple Dot is open until really late on the weekends, where packs of 80 lb. red-faced co-eds can be spotted stumbling around in their glittery halter tops. The restaurant's decor may remind one of a Hong Kong style Mickey Mouse Club, with its colorful curve

voyage.name: Sichuanese Cuisine
voyage.content: The name in Chinese is Lao Sichuan (Old Sichuan Restaurant). Great dry-fried beans with chicken. Simple hotpot and tasty dumplings.

voyage.name: Szechuan Noodle Bowl
voyage.content: The name of the shop in Chinese means "Great King of Beef Noodles". Hole-in-the wall place. Limited selection of spicy noodle soups. Also provides dumplings.

voyage.name: Tai Tung
voyage.content: This restaurant has been open since 1935 and is now the oldest Chinese restaurant in Seattle. It is run and owned by Harry Chan, who is the 3rd generation to continuously operate the restaurant. Look for the table where one-time regular Bruce Lee liked to sit.

voyage.name: Fuji Sushi
voyage.content: Smaller pieces and a bit pricier, but fresh and tasty.

voyage.name: Itsumono
voyage.hours: Lunch Tue-Fri 11:30AM-2PM, dinner Tue-Thu, Sun 5PM-9PM, Fri-Sat 5PM-10PM; Mon closed
voyage.content: Family-run pub with a homely menu and atmosphere. Get your favorite Japanese entrées like tempura, teriyaki, donburi, noodles, and sushi (or an obento with an assortment of everything), or have some beer or shochu and linger for a while ordering small plates.

voyage.name: Maneki
voyage.content: Very good sushi, as well as many non-sushi Japanese dishes. The restaurant claims to be at least 100 years old, although it has moved since its estimated founding date in 1904, and is considerably smaller than the grand space it occupied prior to World War II. Their sushi pieces are very large, and their prices are very reasonable. It is highly suggested to reserve on the day before you wish to eat here.

voyage.name: Salumi
voyage.content: Salami sandwiches on artisan bread... can't beat it. There is often a line that can take over an hour to get through.

voyage.name: Tamarind Tree
voyage.content: At the back of a steep and congested parking lot, three Vietnamese brothers created an atmosphere that feels like a Belltown Hotel than a rough Vietnamese strip mall, with a cool contemporary-style fountain. Try the fish paste with bacon, the spring rolls with a side of fresh peanut sauce, or the seven courses of beef. High quality service, sauces, and appetizers, served up artfully at Little Saigon prices.

voyage.name: Oasis Tea Zone
voyage.content: Pool tables, Ikea furniture, and music videos entertain a mostly younger crowd. Oasis is known for its more fragrant-tasting bubble teas; specifically, they make fruit teas with real fruit.

voyage.name: Panama Hotel Tea & Coffee House
voyage.content: The result of a unique renovation, Panama Hotel is both a teahouse and historical museum. Fine tea connoisseurs appreciate the wide selection of quality teas. The Panama Hotel once housed the personal belongings of interned Japanese Americans who had to sell their homes and abandon their businesses. The belongings that were never claimed, including pieces of furniture and a piano, are on display here.

voyage.name: Zeitgeist
voyage.content: Elegant and arty.

voyage.name: Flatstick Pub
voyage.content: Pub with an indoor underground minigolf course.

voyage.name: Best Western Plus Pioneer Square
voyage.content: Built in 1920 and refurbished a number of times, it's the most decent hotel in the Pioneer Square area. Rooms are compact but breakfast are generous.

voyage.name: Hostelling International Seattle
voyage.content: Offers free breakfast, free WiFi. Excellent common areas including a library, TV room, computer room and clean, spacious kitchen facilities. The location isn't the greatest, given the grit outside.

voyage.name: Panama Hotel
voyage.content: Private, old-fashioned rooms, modest but clean, with bathrooms down the hall. Very relaxing tea and coffee house (see above), with free wireless internet connections. On the street level.

voyage.name: Discovery Park
voyage.content: The largest park in the city can be thought of as Seattle's unofficial central park given its huge, somewhat secluded nature, with a number of trails that meander through the green forests down to the lighthouse at the beach. Discovery Park used to be an army installation called Fort Lawton, and several of the fort's buildings remain. The park features the highest point in the city and wildlife you don't typically fi

voyage.name: Kerry Park
voyage.content: A photographer's paradise, this is perhaps the most obvious spectacle in Queen Anne. This park affords the quintessential view of Downtown Seattle with the Space Needle in the foreground, and (depending on the weather) Mount Rainier and the Cascades, as well as across the Puget Sound to Bainbridge Island.

voyage.name: Bhy Kracke Park
voyage.content: Pronounced "By Crackie". You can get a view comparable to that from the Space Needle for free.

voyage.name: Fishermen's Terminal
voyage.content: Carefully wander the docks (avoiding stepping on ropes or nets) and look at the boats. Many of them sell fresh crab or fish right off of the boat in season. Much of the Alaska crab fishing fleet moors here (or elsewhere in Lake Union) during the off-season, including vessels featured in the long-running Deadliest Catch television series. Visit the Fishermen's Memorial dedicated to all of those who have lost their liv

voyage.name: Space Needle
voyage.price: standard admission is $55 (discounts of up to $20 per ticket if reservation made at lease 1 day in advance)
voyage.content: A symbol of Seattle, built for the 1962 World's Fair and still a wildly popular attraction. The view is spectacular on a clear day when the sun sets, when Downtown Seattle contrasts beautifully with the ocean to the west and the snow-capped mountains in every other direction. There are floor-to-ceiling windows on both levels, a rotating glass floor ("The Loupe") on the lower level that completes one revolution every

voyage.name: Pacific Science Center
voyage.price: Adults from̩ $22.95-̩$28.20 depending on day. Planetarium and daytime laser shows included, but requires timed tickets
voyage.content: An interactive science museum featuring permanent and temporary exhibits, a butterfly atrium, IMAX theater, planetarium, and laser shows.

voyage.name: Museum of Pop Culture
voyage.price: $28 adults, $25 seniors/students, $22 military, $19 youth, children 4 and under free. $2 discount if purchased online. Additional $8 for special exhibit. Outdoor playground free
voyage.hours: Summer (Memorial Day-Labor Day) 10AM-7PM daily; rest of year 10AM-5PM daily
voyage.content: An excellent pop culture museum housed inside a visually striking building designed by Frank Gehry to "evoke the rock 'n' roll experience", with exhibits on all manner of popular culture: film, television, music, video games, fashion, etc. There's a particular focus on science fiction and Seattle musicians, with a sci-fi hall of fame and exhibits dedicated to Jimi Hendrix and Nirvana. Top-notch special exhibits have

voyage.name: Seattle Children's Museum
voyage.price: General exhibits: $7.50, $6.50 seniors, children under 1 free; no adults admitted without a child
voyage.content: An independent non-profit museum which hosts popular traveling exhibits and features permanent exhibits and programs geared towards children.

voyage.name: Chihuly Garden and Glass
voyage.price: $19 adults, $17 seniors, $12 children, children 3 and under free
voyage.hours: Mon-Thu 10AM–10PM, Fri-Sun 10AM-11PM; last ticket sold one hour prior to closing; combined tickets with Space Needle available
voyage.content: This museum provides a look at the inspiration and influences that inform the career of artist Dale Chihuly. The on-site exhibition hall contains eight galleries and three drawing walls, offering visitors a comprehensive look at Chihuly’s significant series of work. The centerpiece of the museum is a glasshouse with a suspended 1,400-piece, 100-foot-long sculpture. Also on the grounds is a lush garden, which serves a

voyage.name: Lake Union Park
voyage.content: Home to the Center for Wooden Boats and the Museum of History and Industry. Spray park open Memorial Day to Labor Day.

voyage.name: The Center for Wooden Boats
voyage.hours: Opens daily at 10AM except Mondays November through mid-April; closing hours vary by season. Free boat sails Sun 10AM (signup), 11AM-3PM (cruise)
voyage.content: An intriguing museum where you can learn about maritime culture and experience sailing traditional wooden boats. The center's programs allow you to get a hands-on feel, putting in control of crafting and sailing your own wooden craft. On Sundays, rain or shine, you can get a free boat ride on a classic wooden boat around the lake for an hour. At times artist-in-residence Saaduuts leads programs.

voyage.name: Museum of History and Industry
voyage.price: $25 adults, $20 seniors, children under 14 free; free first Thursday of the month
voyage.content: The museum focuses on the history of Seattle and the greater Puget Sound region, with exhibitions focusing on the maritime history of the city and the rise of the region's technology industry, as well as a set of changing exhibits.

voyage.name: Northwest Seaport/Maritime Heritage Center
voyage.content: Home to a number of historic ships, including a schooner, a tugboat, a fireboat, a lightship, a steamer, and several others.

voyage.name: South Lake Union Discovery Center
voyage.content: An introduction to the neighborhood, with displays explaining the history of South Lake Union. There is also a model of the whole neighborhood in the building.

voyage.name: Amazon HQ tour
voyage.content: 90-minute tour of Amazon's urban campus including Doppler, Day 1, and the Spheres. There is also a self-guided audio tour; you can even get a free pair of headphones to keep from the receptionists at Day 1 (2121 7th Ave; M-F 7AM-6PM).

voyage.name: Seattle Spheres
voyage.price: Free; reservations required, available 30 days in advance
voyage.content: A building made of three glass domes filled with lush plants. Take an unguided stroll through the tropical heart of the Spheres.

voyage.name: Understory
voyage.content: Visitor center about Amazon and the Spheres' flora and design. It's in the bottom floor of the Spheres and doesn't get you access to the upper floors where the plants live, but it's available 5 days a week unlike public access to the building.

voyage.name: Public Art at Amazon Headquarters
voyage.content: While the Amazon buildings are not open to the public, there are several signed outdoor art pieces around the complex and other nearby buildings, and you can hob-nob with "blue badges" at local restaurants and coffee shops. Seattle Architecture Foundation also leads guided walking tours.

voyage.name: Northwest Folklife Festival
voyage.content: A more low-key and global version of Bumbershoot.

voyage.name: Bite of Seattle
voyage.content: Part of the Seafair festivities.

voyage.name: Bumbershoot
voyage.content: A music and arts festival featuring dozens of local and world-class musical acts.

voyage.name: Seattle Center WinterFest
voyage.hours: Late Nov to late Dec or early Jan
voyage.content: Various activities/events during the holidays such as the WinterFest Ice rink (skate rental available for fee), Winter Train & Village, ice sculpting displays.

voyage.name: Festál Cultural Center
voyage.content: Celebrate the world with festivals from about 25 countries represented, one country nearly every 2 weeks.

voyage.name: Climate Pledge Arena
voyage.content: The region's largest sports arena is home to the NHL's Seattle Kraken, the WNBA's Seattle Storm, and college men's basketball games of the Seattle Redhawks (Seattle University), as well as a major concert venue. It was built for the 1962 World's Fair. The arena's interior was completely gutted and rebuilt for the Kraken, but its original exterior remains intact, maintaining its historic listing. Tours not available;

voyage.name: McCaw Hall
voyage.content: Home of the Seattle Opera and the Pacific Northwest Ballet, each considered among the best in the United States.

voyage.name: Seattle Repertory Theatre
voyage.hours: Box officeː Mon-Fri noon-5PM, by phone noon-6PM
voyage.content: The largest nonprofit resident theatre in the Pacific Northwest.

voyage.name: Seattle International Film Festival (SIFF)
voyage.content: One of the largest film festivals in North America. Screenings are at the w:SIFF Cinema Uptown, SIFF Film Center, and at venues in adjacent districts.

voyage.name: SIFF Cinema Uptown
voyage.content: Three-screen theater showing art, indie, and foreign films and documentaries.

voyage.name: Lake Union Crew
voyage.content: A club boathouse for the local rowing community. If you have no rowing experience, classes are offered.

voyage.name: Northwest Outdoor Center
voyage.content: Kayak and paddleboard rentals.

voyage.name: The Electric Boat Company
voyage.content: Electric boat rentals for up to 12 passengers. Offers enclosed and heated vessels for year-round appeal. No prior experience needed.

voyage.name: Queen Anne Farmers' Market
voyage.address: Queen Ave N & W Crockett St
voyage.content: Farmers market with food booths and vendors selling crafts up on Queen Anne Hill

voyage.name: South Lake Union Saturday market
voyage.content: Farmers market with food booths and vendors selling crafts.

voyage.name: Play It Again Sports
voyage.content: New and secondhand sports equipment, usually in excellent condition. Skis and snowboards, bikes, and a small assortment of other sporting goods.

voyage.name: REI Flagship Store
voyage.content: Recreation Equipment Inc., the large outdoors equipment retailer, was founded in Seattle in 1938. REI's sprawling flagship store has an outdoor trail for test-driving mountain bikes, a climbing wall, and a small "mountain" in the shoe section for trying hiking boots. It also has a clearance section where you can often find boots, down sleeping bags, tents, etc. with easily repairable damage at a fraction of the cost.

voyage.name: Community Banana Stand
voyage.content: A fruit stand offering free bananas to passersby, operated by Amazon from its headquarters. The stand gives away thousands of bananas each weekday, as a cheap and convenient way to give a little boost to employees and the general public alike.

voyage.name: Art Marble 21
voyage.content: American cuisine and prime sports viewing. Large game room with free arcade games, billiards, giant Jenga, cornhole, bocce ball, and more.

voyage.name: Molly Moon's Homemade Ice Cream
voyage.content: Molly Moon's offers 14 flavors of ice cream, homemade on the premises within sight of the customers. One vegan option is usually offered. Many staff have learned some basic American Sign Language.

voyage.name: Canlis
voyage.content: Seattle's longstanding fine dining restaurant, with a wonderful view overlooking Lake Union and Queen Anne Hill. Live piano music. Make reservations well in advance (a week or two ahead) and dress well; it's one of the few Seattle establishments with a strict dress code.

voyage.name: Caffe Fiore
voyage.content: An organic coffeeshop three blocks north of Kerry Park, offering a true experience of Seattle coffee house culture: good local art on display that changes on the first day of every month, consistently excellent coffee, environmental consciousness to a fault (the straws are compostable), and neighborly vitality that's easy to witness but hard to describe. Handsome baristas remember the orders of regular patrons, and m

voyage.name: Top Pot Doughnuts
voyage.content: Lodged in a former neighborhood grocery, this place offers "hand-forged" doughnuts, coffee, juice, and the like. Free wireless available.

voyage.name: Macrina Bakery
voyage.content: A premier local bakery whose chef was a finalist for a 2007 James Beard Award. Selection changes seasonally and daily, but there's always something delicious on offer. An excellent choice for a breakfast or light lunch; cafe-style seating encourages you to sit down and stay a while. Espresso can be inconsistent, if you're picky, grab food to go and walk elsewhere for coffee.

voyage.name: Ozzie's
voyage.content: Karaoke is the name of the game at Ozzie's and is available every night starting at 9PM.

voyage.name: Toulouse Petit Kitchen & Lounge
voyage.content: Excellent restaurant and lounge featuring New Orleans-style food and drink that was listed as a 2012 Travelers Choice Awards winner for one of America's best restaurants and one of the best happy hours in the USA by CNBC survey (great beignets). Happy hour every day from 4PM to 6PM and 10PM to 1AM with a breakfast happy hour from Monday to Friday from 8AM to 11AM.

voyage.name: Homewood Suites by Hilton Seattle
voyage.content: All-suite hotel with views of Elliott Bay.

voyage.name: MarQueen Hotel
voyage.content: Boutique lodging accommodations.

voyage.name: The Maxwell Hotel
voyage.content: Unique dog and earth-friendly lodging with a business center, free parking, and views of the Space Needle.

voyage.name: Travelodge Seattle Center
voyage.content: Two blocks east of the Space Needle and monorail terminal, adjacent to Belltown. About a mile's walk (or a few minutes on the monorail) from the downtown core.

voyage.name: Northwest Nikkei Museum
voyage.alt: Japanese Cultural Community Center of Washington
voyage.content: Small exhibits relating to the history of nikkei (Japanese immigrants) in the Pacific Northwest.

voyage.name: Seattle Asian Art Museum
voyage.price: $15/adult, $13/seniors, $13/military, $10/student, children free, last Fridays free, all tickets +$3 if not bought in advance
voyage.content: An offshoot of downtown's Seattle Art Museum, SAAM displays a portion of the permanent collection balanced with rotating, consistently well-curated special exhibitions. The focus is usually on Chinese or Japanese art, reflecting long-established ties across the Pacific, but does include works from as far as India and the Middle East. The Art Deco building (the Seattle Art Museum's original home) is an attraction in i

voyage.name: Frye Art Museum
voyage.content: A small private collection of modern art with rotating contemporary exhibitions. Parking is always available and the place is worth a visit.

voyage.name: Cal Anderson Park
voyage.content: A very popular park on sunny days. It includes a signature fountain and pond, a basketball court, tennis and softball fields, and a playground. Great for peoplewatching, and you can often see groups of people doing activities varying from hackeysack to drum circles to freeze tag to bike polo to twirling around with colorful scarves.

voyage.name: Hot Rat Summer Mosaic
voyage.content: A small tile-and-glass mosaic of a rat in a devotional pose, labeled with its namesake caption. It was illicitly installed on the side of a utility gatehouse in 2024. The city repeatedly tried to remove it, but community members swiftly striped away the paint covering it up amidst a swell of public appreciation for the art, so it was eventually allowed to stay.

voyage.name: Lakeview Cemetery
voyage.content: Incorporated in 1872, Lakeview Cemetery is set on a hillside with views of Lake Union, the Cascades, Lake Washington and the Olympic Mountains. The site holds the final resting places of Seattle's first families, many with diverse backgrounds. Many come to pay tribute at the graves of Bruce Lee and his son Brandon.

voyage.name: Viretta Park
voyage.content: The park's wooden benches are covered with graffiti messages to Nirvana frontman Kurt Cobain, as it is next door to the home where he died in 1994. This is the closest thing in Seattle to a memorial to the rock icon; serious fans should consider a road trip to his childhood hometown of Aberdeen.

voyage.name: Volunteer Park
voyage.content: Designed by John Charles Olmsted and Fredrick Law Olmsted Jr, this is the largest park in Capitol Hill. It is the site of a botanical conservatory and the Seattle Asian Art Museum (above).

voyage.name: Volunteer Park Conservatory
voyage.price: Adult $6; Youth under 18, students, seniors 65+, military $4; children under 6 Free
voyage.content: A Victorian-style greenhouse with thousands of living specimens on display. There are five sections: bromeliads, ferns, palms, seasonal, and cacti/succulents.

voyage.name: Water Tower
voyage.content: The 1906 tower at the highest point of Capitol Hill has an observation deck at the top, with views from the Cascades to the Olympics interspersed with a series of panels explaining the history of Seattle's Olmsted-designed park system. The views are somewhat obstructed by metal grates, but the clever photographer can work around them. No elevator - the only way up is the staircase wound around the water tank, seven s

voyage.name: Washington Park Arboretum
voyage.content: The Arboretum is a 230-acre park additionally serving as a botanical garden and horticultural research center, with thousands of trees and plants from temperate climates represented. An extensive network of walking trails covers the park. The visitor's center, near the northeast corner of the park, is open from 10AM to 4PM daily, and has limited parking available. Guided tours are offered on the first and third Sunda

voyage.name: Seattle Japanese Garden
voyage.price: $6 adults, $4 children over 5 years and seniors
voyage.hours: Hours vary seasonally: generally Tue-Sun 10AM until sunset. Extended hours from May to September, closed December to February; check the link above for more detailed information
voyage.content: A small, formal Japanese garden within the grounds of the Arboretum.

voyage.name: Streissguth Gardens
voyage.address: E Blaine St between 10th Ave E and Broadway E
voyage.content: A small, family-maintained garden on the northwest side of Seattle's Capitol Hill, on a steep hillside. Noisy but offering great views over Lake Union, Downtown Seattle, and the Olympic Mountains in the distance.

voyage.name: Madison Park
voyage.content: Activities include swimming, bathhouse, restaurants, tennis court (with lights), and great views of the floating bridge and the Cascades. Lifeguards patrol the area during the summer, which creates a safer playground for kids, but it's still a beautiful park to hang out for teens and adults.

voyage.name: Jimi Hendrix statue
voyage.content: A life-size bronze sculpture of Hendrix rocks out on the sidewalk. Seattle was the birthplace and childhood home of the influential guitarist.

voyage.name: Seattle University
voyage.content: A private Jesuit university. Scenic campus makes a good walking detour.

voyage.name: Chapel of St. Ignatius
voyage.content: A hidden gem, this small campus chapel was described by architect Stephen Holl as "seven bottles of light in a stone box". It is probably the most notable religious building built in Seattle in the last fifty years.

voyage.name: Hothouse Spa & Sauna
voyage.content: A small urban women-only spa with an industrial/basement vibe. Great for a relaxing soak in the tub. Expect to be nude and quiet, and bring your own towels.

voyage.name: Club Z
voyage.content: On the other end of the spectrum, Club Z is a gay male bathhouse with no tubs and a lot of glory holes! Don't walk in if you expect to do any dancing or, um, bathing.

voyage.name: Club Comedy Seattle
voyage.content: Boutique style stand-up comedy club.

voyage.name: Raygun Lounge
voyage.content: All-ages gaming bar with board games and pinball machines. The atmosphere is more like a dive bar: the beer, cider and wine are good, but the food is mediocre, and the TVs are usually playing B-movies (but sometimes have some good campy sci-fi like Doctor Who).

voyage.name: I-5 Colonnade Mountain Bike Skills Park
voyage.address: Lakeview Blvd E and Harvard Ave E
voyage.content: The bike park was built underneath a section of 12 elevated lanes of Interstate 5. It consists of several mountain bike skills trails, including novice, intermediate, and advanced sections, a dirt jumping section, pump track, and trials area. Skills classes, organized by the Evergreen Mountain Bike Alliance, are occasionally held at the park.

voyage.name: Central Cinema
voyage.content: A unique, smaller movie theater that shows older films as well as plenty of late night movie screenings of hilariously bad films. All seats have table in front of them so you can have excellent food and beer during the show. A couple times a month there are $1.99 movie nights for popular older or cult films.

voyage.name: Northwest Film Forum
voyage.content: A Seattle-based non-profit organization for film artists, showcasing American and international cinema as well as quarterly world premiere live performances.

voyage.name: SIFF Cinema Egyptian
voyage.content: One-screen theater showing art, indie, and foreign films and documentaries.

voyage.name: Seattle International Film Festival (SIFF)
voyage.content: One of the largest film festivals in North America. Screenings are at the SIFF Cinema Egyptian and other SIFF venues in adjacent districts.

voyage.name: Capitol Hill Block Party
voyage.content: This music festival during the height of summer attracts both local and national musicians.

voyage.name: Elliott Bay Book Company
voyage.content: In 2010, Seattle's largest independent bookstore moved up onto the Hill from its old home in Pioneer Square. The wide, wooden-shelved spaces are a pleasure to browse. There's a small cafe tucked in the back of the lower level, which is good but rather expensive.

voyage.name: Twice Sold Tales
voyage.content: Capitol Hill's last remaining used bookstore. A good selection of literature, philosophy and more contemporary reads. Home of numerous cats, who appear to have free rein.

voyage.name: Capitol Hill Farmers Market
voyage.content: This year-round farmers market has local produce and meats, and tasty ready-to-eat foods. In the colder months, try a cup of seafood stew or some tamales.

voyage.name: Big John's PFI
voyage.content: A family-owned specialty importer since 1971. Their shelves are packed with ingredients from Italy and beyond, with an extensive selection of cheeses, olives, spices and wine.

voyage.name: Uncle Ike's Capitol Hill
voyage.content: Large dispensary with bright clean displays. Wide selection of products and accessories for all different forms of consumption, including lots of edibles and beverages.

voyage.name: Uncle Ike's CD
voyage.content: Large dispensary with bright clean displays. Wide selection of products and accessories for all different forms of consumption, including lots of edibles and beverages.

voyage.name: Big Mario's New York Pizza
voyage.content: True New York-style thin crust pizza. Huge, foldable slices or whole pies. Full bar with lots of local beers. Pizza window open late night.

voyage.name: Bakery Nouveau
voyage.content: Everything you'd want from a French-style bakery: pastries, breads, elegant desserts, macarons, chocolate confections by the piece, sandwiches, quiches, and pizzas, plus coffee of course. Very popular; the line often stretches to the door and beyond, but it moves quickly enough. The limited seating is usually pretty full; in a pinch there's a park across the street with a bench of two.

voyage.name: Dick's Drive-In
voyage.content: Where the cool hang out (according to Sir Mix-a-Lot's song "Posse on Broadway"). Dick's is a local fast food staple; perhaps the most iconically "Seattle" restaurant around. The menu is simple: unsophisticated yet satisfying burgers in just a couple of variations (try the Deluxe, it's not that large), hot greasy fries, and tasty hand-dipped milkshakes. Drive up or walk up; this place will be hopping on a Friday or Sa

voyage.name: Ezell's Famous Chicken
voyage.content: This Central District mainstay gained wide renown when Oprah Winfrey declared it her favorite, but it really needs no celebrity endorsements; it's hands-down the best stuff around. This flagship location sits directly across from Garfield High School. There's no seating, but they accept credit cards. Spicy and original; the spicy chicken isn't too spicy, but you can get a side of hot sauce for 11 cents extra. Daily s

voyage.name: Frankie & Jo's
voyage.content: Their coconut-based ice cream is decadently creamy and creatively flavored with seasonal ingredients.

voyage.name: Hot Mama's Pizza
voyage.hours: Sun noon-midnight, Mon-Wed 11AM-midnight, Thu 11AM-2AM, Fri Sat 11AM-2:30AM
voyage.content: Classic New York-style pizza by the slice. You can't go wrong here and the pesto is particularly popular.

voyage.name: Italian Family Pizza
voyage.content: Very good East Coast style pizza with large servings and cheap beer served all day in a restaurant operated by East Coast transplants. Relocated from downtown Seattle to a larger restaurant in First Hill.

voyage.name: Jamjuree
voyage.content: A Thai place that's fairly quiet and upscale, with excellent specials - try the Lime Light Chicken if you have a chance. On request they can make truly vegetarian Thai food (i.e., without fish sauce).

voyage.name: Moonlight Cafe
voyage.content: Serves excellent vegan mock-meat versions of Vietnamese and Chinese dishes such as noodle bowls and sesame beef. In fact, they boast a full vegan menu with as many dishes as their separate carnivorous menu offers.

voyage.name: Ooink
voyage.content: One of several excellent ramen shops in Capitol Hill. Depending on what style of ramen you prefer, you may like others such as Ramen Danbo, Betsutenjin, or Menya Musashi.

voyage.name: Americana
voyage.content: Eclectic menu of American fusion fare and some delicious simple cocktails. Extremely popular on weekends with their large brunch menu and Bloody Marys.

voyage.name: Ayutthaya
voyage.content: Inexpensive, quality Thai food. It specializes in Thai classics such as coconut chicken & drunken noodles, with happy hour.

voyage.name: Ba Bar
voyage.content: A myriad of cocktails plus Vietnamese street fare, which also includes a bakery. Known for its rotisserie meat, pho, banh cuon (rice noodle roll), and macaroons. Open late night with comfort food options. No reservations needed.

voyage.name: Cactus
voyage.content: A local favorite. A creative mix of Mexican, Southwestern and Spanish cuisine complemented by great cocktails. Always full, with outdoor seating in the summer.

voyage.name: Cafe Flora
voyage.content: Upscale, all-vegetarian cuisine in a casual atmosphere. Menus change weekly.

voyage.name: Cafe Lago
voyage.content: Established Italian restaurant popular for vegetarian lasagna, apple-wood fired pizza, and fresh hand-made pasta (they have an employee dedicated solely to making pasta). An excellent environment for families, they even have paper tablecloths for kids to draw on.

voyage.name: Julia's On Broadway
voyage.hours: Mon Tue 11AM-10PM, Wed-Fri 9AM-midnight, Sat 8AM-midnight, Sun 8AM-5PM. Drag shows Thu 8:30PM; Fri 9PM; Sat 1PM, 9PM; Sun 1PM
voyage.content: Julia's serves Northwest cuisine along with good ol' American food, breakfast, lunch and dinner. Average quality, expensive meals and cocktails are prepared in a charming old building that used to house a seriously divey gay bar until they gutted it and put in a tasteful interior. The location is excellent, but the service can be less than stellar. That's because the real attraction is not the food but the drag shows

voyage.name: Monsoon
voyage.hours: Mon-Fri 11:30AM to 3PM, Sun-Thu 5-10PM, Fri Sat 5-11PM, Sat Sun 10AM-3PM
voyage.content: Contemporary Vietnamese dishes (mainly southern Vietnamese) mixed with Pacific Northwest innovation. Dim sum brunches on the weekends.

voyage.name: Pizzeria Pagliacci
voyage.content: Serves unique Seattle-style pizza, reminiscent of thin-crust, by-the-slice New York pizza, but with an imaginative collection of toppings that change with the seasons. Walk in and ask for two slices of "primo" and you won't be disappointed. The Pagliaccio salad is a good starter. There are branches in the University District and Queen Anne, plus delivery throughout the city.

voyage.name: Annapurna Cafe
voyage.content: Perhaps the crown of Seattle's Indian food scene, Annapurna also serves excellent Nepali and Tibetan food. A charming atmosphere, quality food, and a wide variety of vegetarian and vegan options make it a great location for dinner.

voyage.name: Cafe Soleil
voyage.content: A casual and laid-back Ethiopian restaurant, serving both traditional Ethiopian food and adaptations using Northwest ingredients. Housed in a beautiful building with excellent natural light, with outdoor seating as well. Well-stocked with Ethiopian beers.

voyage.name: Carrello
voyage.content: Artisanal Italian food in small portions so you can construct a meal however you like. Carts roll past tables offering cheaper antipasti to supplement your meal or wash down your cocktail.

voyage.name: Taneda
voyage.content: Small Japanese bar serving prix fixe sushi in the style of kaiseki, a traditional multi-course meal consisting of several small dishes. Reservations required, and with only 17 seats and two dinners per night, they are booked up to 2 months in advance.

voyage.name: Caffé Vita
voyage.content: Coffee roaster with a warehouse feel, where patrons can clearly see how the coffee beans are roasted.

voyage.name: Espresso Vivace Roasteria
voyage.content: Founded by an engineer who's been developing progressively more sophisticated roasters for twenty years. Their beans, plus Mighty-O doughnuts, are also available at the sidewalk Vivace at 321 Broadway E, between Harrison and Thomas.

voyage.name: Macrina Cafe & Bakery
voyage.content: A premier local bakery whose chef was a finalist for a 2007 James Beard Award. Selection changes seasonally and daily, but there's always something delicious on offer. An excellent choice for a breakfast or light lunch; cafe-style seating encourages you to sit down and stay a while. Espresso can be inconsistent, if you're picky, grab food to go and walk elsewhere for coffee.

voyage.name: Realfine Coffee
voyage.content: Social coffee-drinking environment.

voyage.name: Broadcast Coffee Roasters
voyage.content: A neighborhood shop serving Stumptown coffee and pastries from Alki Bakery. Free WiFi. Great for meetings.

voyage.name: Top Pot Doughnuts
voyage.content: Nestled into the neighborhood and a favorite weekend hang-out for locals. Incredible doughnuts (try the feather boa doughnut!) in a very Seattle-y atmosphere. Drip coffee isn't so hot, but the freshly-brewed options are all good.

voyage.name: Victrola
voyage.content: Neighborhood place, more spacious than most. Their roastery also has a (smaller) space at 310 E Pike St in Downtown.

voyage.name: Cha Cha Lounge
voyage.content: A weird cross of dive bar and trendy spot, the ambiance of their old location was successfully transplanted to this location after their former building was razed for yet more condo construction. Your bartender may have had an album in the charts circa 1992.

voyage.name: Pine Box
voyage.content: Located in a former funeral home (rumored to have handled Bruce Lee's body) that has now been converted to offices and a beer bar. Enjoy one of the best beer selections in the neighborhood.

voyage.name: DeLuxe Bar and Grill
voyage.content: Dark, but appealing for a beer, stiff drink or bar food (hearty burgers, thick fries, etc.) More restaurant than bar.

voyage.name: Garage
voyage.content: A trendy billiards hall and bowling alley, built in a spacious former garage that has no problem handling large groups. Multiple bars with food service, and an outdoor patio (weather permitting).

voyage.name: Herb & Bitter Public House
voyage.content: An excellent spot for their gourmet and slightly modernist food, but even better for their ever-changing cocktails, expertly designed using seasonal flavors and uncommon ingredients. A patio in the back with a sliding glass roof means you can enjoy the sky view (boxed in by surrounding buildings) rain or shine.

voyage.name: Liberty
voyage.content: Free WiFi, large couches, decent sushi, good drinks and attractive servers conspire to make this one of the better Capitol Hill bars.

voyage.name: Linda's Tavern
voyage.content: The outdoor patio makes this the perfect place to enjoy a few drinks under the stars.

voyage.name: Smith
voyage.content: Another bar owned by Linda Derschang of Linda's fame. Although Smith regularly becomes packed in the evening, large communal tables in the center of the establishment mean you can usually find a place to sit.

voyage.name: Stumbling Monk
voyage.content: Its dark appearance from the outside makes it easy to miss, but worth stepping inside. As the name suggests, you’ll find an excellent selection of Belgian beer strong enough to make your walk home a challenge. The Stumbling Monk’s unpretentious atmosphere makes it a down-to-earth oasis on trendy Capitol Hill.

voyage.name: Summit Public House
voyage.content: Offers many beers on tap and is home to one of the best BLTs in the city.

voyage.name: Rhein Haus
voyage.content: Bavarian beer garden with indoor bocce courts, bratwurst and pretzels.

voyage.name: CC's Seattle
voyage.content: Dark laid-back bar for all types of men, serving strong drinks. Very community oriented; recurring events fill the bar with a big crowd, such as weekly video game nights on Wednesdays, meetups for leather, furry, or nudist groups, and monthly dances with dress codes such as fetish gear or underwear.

voyage.name: Crescent Lounge
voyage.content: Small dive bar with nightly karaoke.

voyage.name: The Cuff Complex
voyage.content: Gay bar and dance club, often attracts a leather crowd.

voyage.name: Diesel
voyage.content: Bear and cub bar.

voyage.name: Madison Pub
voyage.content: Unpretentious and crowded gay sports bar. Pool tables and darts.

voyage.name: Neighbors
voyage.content: Gay dance club. The place to take your straight friends.

voyage.name: The Pony
voyage.content: Small dive bar in an old building with a year-round patio and fire pit. Wide variety of music, and a schedule full of go-go dancers, karaoke, and tea dancing.

voyage.name: Queer/Bar
voyage.content: Inclusive bar with a variety of quality performances, and excellent pub food.

voyage.name: Seattle Eagle
voyage.content: Classic gay leather bar. Underwear parties on Saturdays.

voyage.name: Wildrose
voyage.content: One of the oldest lesbian bars on the West Coast. Very cheap tacos and Tecates on Tuesdays, and cheap well drinks on Thursdays.

voyage.name: Gaslight Inn
voyage.content: Bed and breakfast.

voyage.name: Silver Cloud Hotel Seattle – Broadway
voyage.content: A local chain brand. Rooms are generously spacious. Complete facilities such as complimentary Wi-Fi, a restaurant, gym and swimming pool, which considering the typical price, is a giveaway.

voyage.name: Hotel Sorrento
voyage.content: This historic hotel has crowned the First Hill since 1908. It is a posh, Italianate, 7-story hotel with fine dining in the AAA - 4 diamond Hunt Club - For a classy night out before the "hopera".

voyage.name: Hiram M. Chittenden Locks
voyage.content: Linking the freshwater Lake Union and the salt-water Puget Sound across a height difference of 22 feet, the locks allow boats to cross the Lake Washington Ship Canal, relying solely on the force of gravity. A salmon ladder with a viewing gallery allows visitors to witness the salmon migration, which with different species allow for viewing throughout most of the year, but preferably mid to late summer. Adjacent is th

voyage.name: National Nordic Museum
voyage.price: $20 adults, $16 seniors, $15 college students, $10 children above 5 yrs, under 5 free
voyage.content: Documents the history of Scandinavian immigration to Seattle, with rotating art exhibits and a permanent collection of historical artifacts. Julefest includes discounted admission and a Christmas market.

voyage.name: Edith Macefield "Up" House
voyage.content: Edith Macefield received worldwide attention in 2006 when she turned down an offer of $1 million to sell her house to make way for a five-story commercial development. Instead, the Ballard Blocks project was built surrounding her 108-year-old farmhouse. While production of the film Up, based on a strikingly similar premise, started two years before, Disney acknowledged the story with a promotional tie-in.

voyage.name: Ballard Commons Park
voyage.content: Ballard Commons Park features a playground, skate bowl, water feature, engaging public art, relaxing seating areas and lawns and ADA accessible walkways.

voyage.name: Golden Gardens Park
voyage.content: A wonderful saltwater beach park in Ballard, past the locks and Shilshole Marina. Water around here is too cold to swim except for crazy and determined kids during the hottest months, but you can wade a little, walk the beach, make sand castles, claim a fire pit, and watch wind surfers and ships go by. On clear days there is a magnificent view of the Olympics on the other side of Puget Sound. Kids of all ages have en

voyage.name: Greenlake Park
voyage.content: The focal point of the Green Lake neighborhood. The 2.8 mi loop path around the lake is frequented by cyclists, runners, rollerbladers, and walkers. The lake is swimmer friendly; algae growth and closures were sometimes a problem before 2004, when the City of Seattle performed a comprehensive cleanup, and it is now one of the cleanest public swimming areas in the Seattle area.

voyage.name: Sacred Rain Healing Center
voyage.content: Connect with yourself. Seattle's only indoor/outdoor, all-gender clothing-optional hydrotherapy spa. Therapeutic massage, acupuncture, chiropractic, naturopathic physician, yoga, sacred music, nature-bathing. 18 and older.

voyage.name: Greenwood Classic Car Show
voyage.content: Outdoor car show with all types of cars and food vendors about 1 mile along Greenwood Ave North.

voyage.name: Ballard Seafoodfest
voyage.content: A parade, a salmon barbecue, local musicians and a lutefisk-eating contest. Most businesses along NW Market St participate by holding sidewalk sales.

voyage.name: Greenwood/Phinney Art Walk
voyage.content: Showcases hundreds of local artists.

voyage.name: Julefest
voyage.hours: Typically a Sat and Sun in late November or early December
voyage.content: Discounted admission to the Nordic Museum and a large collection of food, drink, and craft vendors, with live music. A Nordic-inspired Christmas market.

voyage.name: Freakout Festival
voyage.hours: Typically a Thu-Sun period in early November
voyage.content: An annual 4-day underground music festival held at various venues around the neighborhood each November.

voyage.name: Conor Byrne Pub
voyage.content: A small live music venue and bar.

voyage.name: Tractor Tavern
voyage.content: A medium-sized live music venue typically only open during shows

voyage.name: Sunset Tavern
voyage.content: A small live music venue and bar.

voyage.name: Egan's Ballard Jam House
voyage.content: A small intimate music supper club with mostly jazz (vocal and instrumental) and other styles of live music offered. Open mic (vocal jam) every other Wednesday evening.

voyage.name: Ballard Goodwill Store
voyage.content: As long as you're here you might as well see if you can find a bargain or a treasure.

voyage.name: Sonic Boom Records
voyage.content: Record store

voyage.name: Pema Kharpo
voyage.content: Exotic Tibetan, Nepali and Buddhist items coming straight from the region. Get ready for the smell of incense and a greeting from one of the two female owners as you enter.

voyage.name: Snapdoodle Toys
voyage.content: The most complete toy store in Seattle, with a huge selection for both kids and adults. Don't expect your typical fast food toy giveaways. Formerly Top Ten Toys, sold to Snapdoodle but basically the same store in spirit with the same merchandise.

voyage.name: Phinney Books
voyage.content: A local neighborhood institution; carries a well-curated selection of books across many categories, including children's books.

voyage.name: Seattle ReCreative
voyage.content: A really cool creative reuse shop selling tons of repurposed materials (yarn, fabric, art supplies, even recyclables) and donated books.

voyage.name: Couth Buzzard Books
voyage.content: A bookstore selling both new and used books; accepts trade-ins. They also have a small cafe and feature events and concerts.

voyage.name: The Fiber Gallery
voyage.content: Greenwood's LYS (local yarn store) has a wide variety of quality yarn, notions, tools and books. It offers online knitting classes as well.

voyage.name: Labels Consignment Clothing
voyage.content: Women's consignment store with good quality women's clothing, shoes and accessories.

voyage.name: Bad Albert's Tap & Grill
voyage.content: Cheap yet good quality pub grub: burgers, excellent fries, hot sandwiches, soups and salads.

voyage.name: Gordito's Healthy Mexican Food
voyage.content: Huge servings, a fast but sometimes long line, way-cheap prices, amazingly tasty burritos that most folks can't finish in one sitting (the "Baby burrito" is about the size of an actual baby), lots of homemade salsas (on the salsa bar), and an outdoor patio.

voyage.name: Larsen's Danish Bakery
voyage.content: Famous throughout Seattle, this is the best Scandinavian-style bakery in town.

voyage.name: Mike's Chili Parlor
voyage.hours: Mon-Thu 11AM-11PM, Fri 11AM-midnight, Sat noon-midnight, Sun noon-6PM
voyage.content: Located just east of the Ballard bridge, this combination dive tavern/chili parlor is a good place to grab a spicy, cheap meal. They do chili burgers and dogs too. Cash only!

voyage.name: Red Mill Burgers
voyage.content: Good old-fashioned burgers, fries, and shakes with both indoor and outdoor seating. Cash or card, closed Mondays.

voyage.name: El Moose
voyage.content: Authentic Mexican cooking from Mexico. Try the pork carnitas.

voyage.name: Taquería Tequila Authentic Mexican Food
voyage.content: The name might be deceiving, but this place takes its Mexican food just as seriously as it takes being a place to drink. Cheap burritos, tacos, quesadillas, fajitas.

voyage.name: Valhalla Sandwiches
voyage.content: Features tasty sandwiches, tots, beer and cider.

voyage.name: La Carta de Oaxaca
voyage.content: Cheap and good Oaxaca-style Mexican food.

voyage.name: Indian Bistro
voyage.content: Reasonably priced and delicious. Friendly owner and a definite go-to for any Indian food lover.

voyage.name: Lockspot Cafe
voyage.content: This is an old breakfast and lunch (burgers, mostly) spot that's mostly patronized by local workers and very popular with them.

voyage.name: Matador
voyage.content: Somewhat pricier, more upscale Tex-Mex fare, though their happy-hour bar food menu is more reasonable.

voyage.name: Delancey
